findings.headline: Hines Meadow Car Park has ongoing security costs of £0.225m per annum; only 6 months budgeted, creating £0.113m additional pressure if alternative not found
findings.detail: Ongoing security requirements at Hines Meadow Car Park estimated at approximately £0.225m per annum at current levels. Forecast currently includes only six months of expenditure while alternative operating arrangements assessed. Failure to find sustainable solution could result in additional costs later in year.
findings.matters: Ongoing, unresolved facilities issue. Council has not yet found sustainable solution and is running out of budget for current year. Full annual cost £0.225m if not addressed.
findings.figures: £0.225m per annum ongoing cost, £0.113m additional pressure for unbudgeted half-year
findings.quote: Ongoing security requirements at Hines Meadow Car Park are estimated to cost approximately £0.225m per annum at current levels. The forecast currently includes six months of expenditure while alternative operating arrangements are assessed. Failure to identify a more sustainable solution could result in additional costs later in the year.

findings.headline: Local Authority Housing Fund Round 3 grant utilisation at risk from RSL delivery delays; could lose 8 temporary accommodation properties worth £0.016m per annum each
findings.detail: LAHF R3 project at risk of not utilising government grant within revised timeframe due to Registered Social Landlord delivery not progressing at required pace. If grant not spent, it will be returned and council loses opportunity to develop 8 temporary accommodation properties.
findings.matters: Lost opportunity: grant must be returned if unspent and revenue savings (£0.128m per annum in TA cost reduction) will not be realised. Shows council unable to deliver capital projects.
findings.figures: £0.128m total opportunity (8 properties × £0.016m per annum)
findings.quote: There is a risk that delays on this project wrth the Registered Social Landlord could lead to the Local Authority Housing Fund (LAHF R3) government grant not being fully utilised within the revised timeframe. This could result in the return of grant funding and lost opportunity of 8 temporary accommodation properties each worth £0.016m per annum.

findings.headline: From 2026/27, Disabled Facilities Grant underspends cannot be carried forward and unspent funding will be recovered by MHCLG
findings.detail: Verbal MHCLG guidance indicates DFG underspends will no longer be permitted to be carried forward from 2026/27 onwards and any unspent funding may be recovered. This removes flexibility council has previously used to accommodate project delays in delivering planned housing adaptations.
findings.matters: Policy change directly affects DFG programme management. Removal of carryforward flexibility means council must maintain tighter delivery schedules or risk losing government funding.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: verbal MHCLG guidance indicates that DFG underspends will no longer be permitted to be carried forward from 2026/27 onwards and any unspent funding may be recovered, resulting in reduced flexibility to accommodate project delays similar to those previously seen when delivering planned housing adaptations.

findings.headline: Multiple capital projects experiencing delays and cost growth: Maidenhead Hub slipped to 2027/28, Mill Place Electricity facing injunction and infrastructure complexity
findings.detail: Maidenhead Community Hub project delayed; delivery now forecast to move into 2027/28. Mill Place Electricity Substation faces delays due to pending injunction and discovery of more complex infrastructure than anticipated. Surveys identified cost growth from asset age and previously unknown subsurface elements.
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage and cost growth indicate delivery challenges and rising project costs. Affects council's ability to deliver planned schemes and may require additional funding.
findings.figures: £0.264m (Maidenhead), £0.199m (Mill Place)
findings.quote: There is a risk that the Maidenhead Community Hub (St Clouds) project may experience further delays and funding challenges as the scheme develops. While a new external partner is supporting the project and detailed plans are being progressed, delivery is now forecast to move into 2027/28.

findings.headline: NHS Frimley ICB merger into Thames Valley ICB creates risk that efficiency savings will reduce funding available for social care packages
findings.detail: Merger of Frimley ICB into Thames Valley ICB expected to deliver significant NHS efficiency savings. Risk that organisational changes could reduce funding available to support eligible social care packages, increasing pressure on council's adult social care budget.
findings.matters: Adult social care is major budget area. NHS commissioning changes directly affect funding for eligible service users. Merger creates structural uncertainty about future funding levels.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Recent changes to NHS commissioning arrangements, including the merger of Frimley ICB into Thames Valley ICB, are expected to deliver significant efficiency savings for the NHS. There is a risk that these organisational changes could reduce funding available to support eligible social care packages.

findings.headline: Falling school pupil numbers in Windsor and Ascot creating pressure on budgets with risk of increasing maintained school deficit recovery plans
findings.detail: Falling rolls, particularly in Windsor and Ascot, place ongoing pressure on school budgets. Risk of increasing number of maintained schools requiring deficit recovery plans, with potential implications for long-term school sustainability.
findings.matters: Falling rolls create structural budget pressures that persist. Schools requiring deficit recovery create medium-term sustainability risk and potential need for council intervention.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Falling pupil numbers, particularly in Windsor and Ascot, continue to place pressure on school budgets. There is a risk that an increasing number of maintained schools may require deficit recovery plans, with potential implications for the long-term sustainability of some schools.

findings.headline: SEND Reform Plan approval critical for High Needs Stability Grant and management of historic DSG deficits; funding beyond 2026/27 uncertain
findings.detail: Council's SEND Reform Plan approval is critical for securing High Needs Stability Grant funding and managing historic DSG deficits. Although 2026/27 grant confirmed, funding beyond that remains unannounced and may be insufficient. National guidance on key reform requirements still incomplete.
findings.matters: SEND is significant budget area with known historic deficits. Uncertainty about plan acceptance and future funding creates material financial risk.
findings.figures: None disclosed
findings.quote: Approval of the Council's SEND Reform Plan remains critical to securing High Needs Stability Grant funding and supporting the management of historic DSG deficits. National guidance on key reform requirements remains incomplete.

findings.headline: UASC grant funding shortfall of £0.750m in forecast, expected to increase as more young people reach age 18 attracting lower grant rates
findings.detail: Home Office grant for unaccompanied asylum seeking children is insufficient to cover full cost of local cohort. Council already reflects £0.750m pressure in forecast but expects this to rise as proportion of 18+ young people increases, as they attract lower levels of grant funding.
findings.matters: UASC is mandatory service. Standing structural gap between grant and cost means council must fund growing shortfall from own resources, constraining budget flexibility.
findings.figures: £0.750m currently in forecast, expected to increase
findings.quote: Funding provided through the Home Office for Unaccompanied Asylum Seeking Children may be insufficient to fully meet the cost of supporting the local cohort. This risk has increased as a greater proportion of supported young people are aged 18 and over and attract lower levels of grant funding.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation under pressure from Renters Reform Act and no-fault eviction abolition, with range of £0 to £1.0m impact
findings.detail: The Renters Reform Act is expected to increase both TA demand and costs (£0 to £0.600m pressure), while abolition of no-fault evictions has already driven spike in applications ahead of implementation (£0 to £0.400m pressure). However, increased social housing availability in H2 could offset costs (£0 to £0.300m saving).
findings.matters: TA is mandatory service with high costs and demand-driven by legislative change beyond council control. Material range of outcomes creates significant planning uncertainty for a lender.
findings.figures: £0.600m (Renters Reform Act), £0.400m (demand), £0.300m (social housing offset)
findings.quote: Changes arising from the Renters Reform Act may place additional pressure on the private rented sector, potentially increasing both temporary accommodation demand and accommodation costs.

findings.headline: Savings delivery on track at 98.6% of target, with only £0.087m at high risk despite operating under significant financial pressure.
findings.detail: The council is forecasting delivery of £6.301m of the £6.388m savings target, equivalent to 98.6% achievement. Only £0.087m (all within Place Directorate) is assessed as being at high risk of non-delivery. This positive performance demonstrates some financial discipline despite the council operating under significant financial pressure with multiple demand-led service overspends.
findings.matters: Achievement of cost control targets provides confidence that the council can enforce financial discipline. A lender needs assurance that efficiency programmes are being delivered even under adverse conditions.
findings.figures: Savings target £6.388m; forecast delivery £6.301m (98.6%); high-risk non-delivery £0.087m (1.4%)
findings.quote: Based on current forecasts, this would result in the delivery of £6.301m of savings, equivalent to 98.6% of the annual target. Of the total savings target of £6.388m, savings of £0.087m are currently assessed as being at high risk of non-delivery.

findings.headline: Corporate bad debt provision requirement stands at £6.816m against current provision of £5.779m, with Adult Social Care debt of £7.737m.
findings.detail: Total overdue corporate debt stands at £11.159m, with £5.743m outstanding for more than 12 months. The required bad debt provision is £6.816m but current provision is only £5.779m, creating a shortfall of £1.037m. Adult Social Care represents £7.737m of total debt (69%), including significant outstanding balances from the Integrated Care Board where recovery is delayed. The council has implemented enhanced collection actions but major debtor recovery remains ongoing.
findings.matters: Rising bad debt provisions indicate collection risk. A shortfall between required and actual provision means either the balance sheet is overstated or future budgets will absorb unexpected charges.
findings.figures: Total debt £11.159m; debt >1 year £5.743m; required provision £6.816m; current provision £5.779m; provision gap £1.037m; ASC debt £7.737m
findings.quote: The value of overdue debt held on the corporate ledger, including deferred payment arrangements, stood at £11.159m at Month 4, a reduction from £11.432m reported at Month 2. Of this total, £5.743m relates to debts outstanding for more than 12 months

findings.headline: Treasury management delivering £1.403m borrowing cost underspend through securing rates below budget assumptions.
findings.detail: The non-service budget underspend of £2.210m is principally due to active treasury management. Borrowing has been secured at rates below those assumed in the budget, generating a forecast underspend of £1.403m. Reduced capital expenditure (from slippage) has also generated a Minimum Revenue Provision underspend of £0.281m. Investment income is forecast to exceed budget by £0.161m. However, this treasury gain masks underlying service overspends of £0.889m.
findings.matters: Effective treasury management in a rising rate environment demonstrates active cash management. However, a lender should note this underspend offsets service overspends and should not be assumed to repeat.
findings.figures: Borrowing cost underspend £1.403m; MRP underspend £0.281m; investment income over-delivery £0.161m
findings.quote: This is principally due to lower borrowing costs, generating a forecast underspend of £1.403m. This reflects both lower-than-anticipated capital expenditure and the benefits of active treasury management, with recent borrowing secured at rates below those assumed in the budget.

findings.headline: Children's Services facing £1.423m pressure from new statutory duties requiring grant-funded budget reallocation.
findings.detail: Children's Services is forecasting an overspend of £0.820m (adverse from Month 2 by £0.780m). A review found that grant funding expected to support wider service budgets must instead be directed to meeting direct costs of new statutory duties including Families First reforms and support for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children. This creates a forecast pressure of £1.423m. Excluding this grant reallocation, the directorate would forecast a favourable variance of £0.619m, largely from lower placement costs (372 children in current care vs 406 budgeted).
findings.matters: New statutory duties creating unfunded pressures indicate structural budget challenges that cannot be solved through efficiency measures alone. This pattern signals future deficits unless funding is increased.
findings.figures: Grant-related pressure £1.423m; service overspend £0.820m; placement cost underspend (excluding grant issue) £0.619m
findings.quote: This review has identified a forecast pressure of £1.423m, principally relating to the Families First reforms, care leaver services and support for unaccompanied asylum-seeking children

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £31.152m (38% of council-controlled schemes), with major delays to Waste Collection Vehicles, Heatherwood Royal and other projects.
findings.detail: Forecast slippage has increased from £12.378m at Month 2 to £31.152m at Month 4, equivalent to 38% of the council-controlled programme (similar to 2025/26 outturn of 37%). Major projects affected include Waste Collection Vehicles (now expected predominantly in 2027/28, requiring an additional £7.164m General Fund financing), Heatherwood Royal, Street Lighting Enhancement, Bus Service Improvement Plan and Great Park Link. Capital spend to date is only 7.7% of forecast outturn.
findings.matters: Slippage of this magnitude indicates project delivery challenges and delays in realizing planned outcomes. A lender needs confidence in the council's ability to deliver major capital schemes on time and within budget.
findings.figures: Total slippage £31.152m; council-controlled slippage £16.487m; Waste Collection Vehicles increased council funding by £7.164m
findings.quote: Forecast slippage has increased from £12.378m at Month 2 to £31.152m at Month 4. Of this total, forecast slippage within Council-controlled projects has increased from £3.001m to £16.487m.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend of £0.904m driven by high-cost placements and £0.629m bad debt provision increase from NHS reorganization delays.
findings.detail: ASC is forecasting an overspend of £0.904m, an adverse movement from a balanced position at Month 2. Demand pressures in Learning Disabilities and Mental Health have increased, including a single placement costing £0.340m annually (£6,500 per week). The bad debt provision has increased by £0.629m due to delays recovering income from the Integrated Care Board following NHS reorganization across Berkshire, Surrey and Hampshire. Total ASC debt stands at £7.737m.
findings.matters: A lender needs to track the trajectory of adult social care costs and assess income recovery risks. Both demand growth and income collection issues present material risk to budget stability.
findings.figures: ASC overspend £0.904m; bad debt provision increase £0.629m; high-cost placement £0.340m p.a. (£6,500 weekly); total ASC debt £7.737m
findings.quote: For example, one recent placement for a young person with learning disabilities has an estimated annual cost of £0.340m (£6,500 per week).

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit projected at £17.501m by March 2027, with High Needs SEND spending £9.626m over allocation.
findings.detail: The DSG is forecast to overspend by £8.877m in 2026/27 (expenditure £203.844m against income £195.006m), driven by High Needs Block pressures covering 1,389 children and young people with Education, Health and Care Plans. The cumulative deficit including prior years reaches £17.501m. The Department for Education has introduced a High Needs Stability Grant that could reduce this to £9.739m if the council's SEND Reform Plan is approved—that plan received positive initial feedback in June 2026, but the grant remains subject to the council successfully delivering reform.
findings.matters: A lender must establish whether this unfunded statutory obligation represents a recurring structural deficit or can be managed through government support. The partial relief is materially helpful but uncertain.
findings.figures: In-year DSG deficit £8.877m; cumulative deficit £17.501m; potential High Needs Stability Grant relief £7.762m; High Needs Block variance £9.626m
findings.quote: Expenditure funded through the ringfenced Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) is forecast to exceed the 2026/27 funding allocation by £8.877m. Total expenditure is forecast at £203.844m, compared with grant income of £195.006m.

findings.headline: Place services are delivering significant underspends that are offsetting social care overspends, but this masks an underlying deterioration in total service budget control.
findings.detail: Place budgeted at £25,674k is forecast to underspend by £545k, driven largely by Neighbourhood Services underspending £829k. However, service budgets overall are forecast to overspend by £889k at M4, up £1,090k from M2. The total operating budget position has deteriorated by £717k since M2. The Place underspends are partially offsetting overspends elsewhere, but the overall trend is negative.
findings.matters: While Place underspends are positive, the month-on-month deterioration across service budgets (£1,090k worsening) indicates systemic pressure growing in the second half of the financial year. A lender would interpret this as declining controllability: the council is losing rather than gaining grip on budget.
findings.figures: Total Service & Contingency overspend £889k at M4 (change from M2 £1,090k). Place underspend £545k. Total Operating Budget deterioration since M2: £717k.

findings.headline: Adults & Health and Children's Social Care are running material overspends that emerged or grew substantially between month 2 and month 4.
findings.detail: Adults & Health budgeted at £64,391k is forecast to spend £65,295k (overspend £904k), with the entire overspend emerging between M2 and M4. Children's Social Care is forecast to overspend by £820k, a deterioration of £781k since M2. Together these two core demand-led services account for £1,724k of overspend. The late emergence and rapid growth of these overspends in social care—notoriously difficult to control mid-year—signals pressure or loss of control.
findings.matters: Social care overspends are structural pressures; councils cannot easily cut demand-led services and late-stage growth is harder to address. A lender views rapidly emerging social care overspends as a sign of deteriorating financial management and uncontrollable cost growth.
findings.figures: Adults & Health: budget £64,391k, forecast £65,295k, M4 overspend £904k (change from M2 £904k). Children's Social Care: budget £43,978k, forecast £44,798k, M4 overspend £820k (change from M2 £781k).

findings.headline: The council's budget balances entirely on receipt of £48,754k Exceptional Financial Support funding which has not yet been received by month 4.
findings.detail: The funding section shows "Exceptional Financial Support (48,754)" budgeted as essential income. As of month 4 (late July), this represents 26% of total funding and has not yet been received ("Actuals to Date: 0"). The budget is structured so that without this government support, it would be in deficit. The non-receipt this far into the financial year is a notable risk.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is typically a crisis funding mechanism for councils in financial difficulty. A lender is heavily exposed to the risk that this funding may not be approved or delivered as forecast, which would immediately create a budget crisis.
findings.figures: £48,754k budgeted EFS; £0 received to date; represents 26% of total funding budget of £187,055k
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support (48,754) 0 (48,754) 0 (48,754) 0 0

findings.headline: Cranstoun Relocation tender returns exceeded original budget but final forecast cost improved from month 2 as risks did not materialise.
findings.detail: Original budget £0.800m; month 2 forecast £0.974m (overspend); month 4 forecast £0.878m. Tender returns exceeded original estimate, but overall forecast has reduced since month 2 because some budgeted risks have not occurred and 2027/28 retention payment has been confirmed.
findings.matters: Shows complexity in tender procurement (costs higher than expected initially) but also demonstrates risk management capability and cost discipline as the project has been brought back closer to control.
findings.figures: Original budget £0.800m; month 2 forecast £0.974m; month 4 forecast £0.878m; improvement from month 2 £0.096m
findings.quote: Whilst an overspend has arisen due to tender returns exceeding the original budget estimate, the overall forecast cost has reduced since Month 2 as some budgeted risks have not materialised and the 2027/28 final retention payment has been confirmed. The forecast outturn in 2026/27 is now £0.878m, £0.096m below the Month 2 forecast.

findings.headline: Windsor Leisure Centre De-Carbonisation delivered all planned assets on time with £0.213m underspend achieved through efficient delivery.
findings.detail: Capital project has delivered all planned assets now operational. Forecast slippage of £0.082m reflects only outstanding retention payments. A £0.213m underspend was achieved 'through efficient project delivery and the non-occurrence of budgeted risks', showing both good cost control and risk management.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council can deliver projects on time and under budget when execution is sound; this is the only scheme showing efficient delivery, making it notable against the broader slippage picture.
findings.figures: Forecast underspend £0.213m; forecast slippage (retention) £0.082m
findings.quote: The project has delivered all planned assets, which are now operational. Forecast slippage of £0.082m reflects retention payments yet to be made. A £0.213m underspend has been achieved through efficient project delivery and the non-occurrence of budgeted risks.

findings.headline: Bus Service Improvement Plan slipped by £0.364m because contracted works assessed to exceed what is deliverable in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Budget £0.914m reduced to £0.550m forecast, with £0.364m slipped to 2027/28. Upon consultation with the contract partner, the scope of works was assessed as too large for the year, indicating either overambitious original planning or supplier capacity constraints.
findings.matters: Shows systemic issue: the council cannot deliver contract partner's assessed scope within available time, raising questions about other partnership-based projects and procurement capability.
findings.figures: Budget £0.914m; forecast £0.550m; slippage £0.364m
findings.quote: Upon consultation with the contract partner the works being contracted have been assessed to exceed what is possible within 2026/27 resulting in £0.364m of slippage into 2027-28.

findings.headline: Maidenhead Library external works budget increased by £0.152m (62% increase) due to M4 scope expansion.
findings.detail: Initial budget for Maidenhead Library external works was £0.244m; now forecast at £0.396m. The increase comes from a 'M4 budget proposal for a scope expansion' which the council says will 'allow enhanced control and efficiency' and avoid a proposed future project.
findings.matters: Scope expansion mid-project increases cost and signals either inadequate initial planning or changing requirements; a lender would track whether scope changes become systemic, indicating cost control weaknesses.
findings.figures: Original budget £0.244m; current forecast £0.396m; increase £0.152m (62%)
findings.quote: The increased forecast cost includes the M4 budget proposal for a scope expansion to the Maidenhead Library capital project. The scope increase is expected to allow enhanced control and efficiency with this project and what would have been a proposed project in the future.

findings.headline: £2.349m of High Needs education grant remains unallocated because the council paused project development waiting for DfE SEND reforms; now delayed further pending public consultation.
findings.detail: The council received a High Needs Provision Grant but has not committed the money to specific projects. Development was paused pending DfE policy changes, which have now been released. The council will now develop proposals to bring to Cabinet and public consultation 'later in 2026', meaning allocation and spend is pushed into 2027 or beyond.
findings.matters: A lender would note that grant-funded projects face policy dependency risks and that unallocated grant creates uncertainty about actual capital delivery despite allocated funding, affecting year-to-year forecasting reliability.
findings.figures: £2.349m of High Needs Provision Grant unallocated
findings.quote: There is £2.349m of the received High Needs Provision Grant currently unallocated because the development of projects was paused as the LA waited for the DfE's SEND reforms. Now that these have been released, the LA will develop proposals for capital investment, to bring to Cabinet and then public consultation, later in 2026.

findings.detail: Three major capital schemes totalling £12.237m have moved from budgeted delivery to full-year slippage. Street Lighting Enhancement reduced from £1.678m budget to £0.005m forecast.
findings.matters: Inability to spend on core infrastructure (vehicles, buildings, street works) signals either procurement failure, scope problems, or planning delays that prevent the council from executing its capital strategy.

findings.detail: The single largest slippage item is the £24.355m ICB Health Hub, forecast to deliver only £9.690m, representing a £14.665m underspend. Note 23, which should explain this, is not provided in the document.

findings.matters: Capital slippage affects council's cash flow, ability to deliver promised improvements, and may indicate procurement or project management problems that would concern a lender assessing financial resilience.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet Cleaning Contract Report – Main Report
findings.headline: The estimated annual cost of the new cleaning services contract at £400,000 exceeds the current approved budget of £356,060 by approximately £43,940 (12%), with no explanation of where the additional funding will come from.
findings.detail: The council states its approved budget for the 2026-27 cleaning contract is £356,060 per annum. The procurement exercise estimates the new contract will cost approximately £400,000 per annum—a recurrent annual shortfall of roughly 12%. The paper describes this as a 'realistic reflection of the council's operational requirements' including provision for ad hoc and reactive cleaning, but does not identify how the gap will be funded or whether budgets will be reallocated. Maximum 4-year contract value is £1.6 million.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand how the council will fund an ongoing annual shortfall of £43,940+, whether this will be covered by savings elsewhere, reserve drawdown, or budget reallocation, and whether the budget planning process adequately reflects operational needs.
findings.figures: Approved budget £356,060 per annum; estimated contract value £400,000 per annum; annual shortfall approximately £43,940; maximum 4-year contract value £1.6 million
findings.quote: The £400,000 annual value represents the estimated maximum contract value for approval purposes and does not in itself authorise spend outside approved budgets.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant surplus growing from £8.624m to £17.774m
findings.detail: The schools reserve balance, which tracks DSG surplus and deficit positions, is forecast to increase substantially by £9.15m during 2026-27. This represents a material accumulation of surplus within the schools budget, suggesting either carried-forward surpluses from prior years or current-year overfunding relative to schools' spending.
findings.matters: A growing DSG surplus raises questions about whether schools are being over-funded relative to need, whether surpluses will be clawed back by central government, or whether the council has structural cash-flow flexibility from schools; a lender needs to understand the sustainability and obligations attached to this balance.
findings.figures: Opening balance 8,624; closing balance 17,774 (all figures £000s)
findings.quote: Dedicated Schools Grant (Surplus)/ Deficit 8,624 0 9,150 17,774

findings.headline: The Berkshire Pension Fund moved to cash-flow positive at the 2025 valuation, with contributions now exceeding benefit payments.
findings.detail: The 2025 actuarial valuation found the fund's contributions now exceed pension benefits paid. This is positive news as it means the fund does not require cash injections from the council to pay pensions, and can focus investments on capital growth rather than meeting immediate payment obligations.
findings.matters: A cash-flow positive pension fund reduces the council's immediate financial pressure and risk of unexpected capital calls. This status supports the fund's ability to pursue a long-term investment strategy focused on growth rather than income.
findings.figures: cash-flow positive status from 2025 valuation
findings.quote: At the 2025 actuarial valuation, the Fund was cash-flow positive (contribution receipts exceed the value of pension benefits payable)

findings.headline: The 2025 valuation shows the Berkshire Pension Fund at 86% funding, unchanged from 2022, with full funding targeted by March 2040.
findings.detail: Both the 2022 and 2025 triennial valuations found the fund at 86% funded. The fund has confirmed this as its priority and is developing investment strategy to achieve 100% funding by March 2040. This funding level represents a material deficit in the scheme that affects contribution requirements and the council's pension liabilities.
findings.matters: A pension fund at 86% funding indicates assets fall significantly short of liabilities. This funding gap directly drives contribution rate pressures on scheme employers and represents a material liability for the council as administering authority.
findings.figures: 86% funding level (both 2022 and 2025 valuations), 100% funding target by March 2040
findings.quote: both the 2022 and the 2025 triennial valuations showed the Fund at 86% funded, and the Fund has confirmed its priority to be fully funded by March 2040 at the latest

findings.headline: Scheme employer contributions face a less than 33% probability of exceeding the 35% threshold set as maximum acceptable.
findings.detail: The fund has set a red threshold maximum for employer contributions of 35%, with analysis showing less than 33% probability that projected rates will exceed this in the short-term. Contributions at this level represent a material financial demand on scheme employers, including the council as administering authority.
findings.matters: Pension contribution rates directly impact the council's budget and financial sustainability. The specified risk profile around the 35% threshold indicates material uncertainty about future contribution requirements.
findings.figures: 35% maximum threshold, <33% probability of exceeding
findings.quote: the Fund has set a maximum (red) threshold for total scheme employer contributions of 35% in the short-term, with the likelihood that the project rates exceed that value of less than 33%

findings.paper_title: Berkshire Pension Board Part I Mintues 010926
findings.headline: The Berkshire Pension Fund faces a red-rated risk around workforce resilience and key person dependency, with specialist knowledge concentrated in a small number of officers.
findings.detail: A combined red-rated risk on workforce capacity and succession planning was created. Jo Thistlewood noted that much specialist knowledge was concentrated in a small number of officers and that further work was required to strengthen succession planning and knowledge sharing. Mitigating actions are underway but a full resilience review and workforce strategy remain in development, with capacity constraints limiting progress.
findings.matters: Loss of key pension fund administration staff could disrupt the council's ability to manage its pension obligations and meet regulatory requirements.
findings.figures: Red-rated risk; 96% of active scheme members covered by i-Connect system.
findings.quote: Jo Thistlewood explained that the risk related not to current performance but to ensuring sufficient resilience should key individuals unexpectedly leave or become unavailable. She noted that much specialist knowledge was concentrated within a small number of Officers and that further work was required to strengthen succession planning and knowledge sharing.

findings.paper_title: Berkshire Pension Board Part I Mintues 010926
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation and the proposed creation of the Ridgeway Authority has been identified as a new red-rated risk to the Berkshire Pension Fund with full implications remaining unclear.
findings.detail: Jo Thistlewood reported a new red-rated risk relating to the proposed Ridgeway Authority. The reorganisation could result in transfers of scheme members, assets and liabilities between pension funds with significant governance, funding and investment implications. The Chair emphasised early engagement with relevant authorities to identify appropriate solutions.
findings.matters: Local government restructuring affecting Windsor and Maidenhead could materially alter pension fund governance, the council's obligations and funding arrangements for the council and its scheme members.
findings.figures: New red-rated risk identified; timeline and scope of reorganisation not finalised.
findings.quote: Jo Thistlewood also reported the addition of a new red risk relating to local government reorganisation and the proposed creation of the Ridgeway Authority, noting that while the full implications for the Fund remained unclear, the changes could result in the transfer of scheme members, assets and liabilities between pension funds and would have significant governance, funding and investment implications.

findings.paper_title: Berkshire Pension Board Part I Mintues 010926
findings.headline: A change in the SCAPE discount rate from CPI plus 1.7% to CPI plus 2% reduced pension strain costs for scheme employers without creating additional funding burden.
findings.detail: The SCAPE discount rate increase affected pension calculation factors for transfers, retirement calculations and divorce settlements. Philip Boyton clarified that this change reduced pension strain costs for employers (the costs incurred when employees take early or late retirement) and did not create additional funding burden for the pension fund.
findings.matters: Lower pension strain costs reduce unexpected budget pressures for Windsor and Maidenhead when employees exercise early retirement options.
findings.figures: SCAPE discount rate increased from CPI plus 1.7% to CPI plus 2%.

findings.detail: The Chair noted progress in improving the Fund's funding position across recent valuations and stated that stable contribution rates would be welcomed by scheme employers. Rachel Howard, the s.151 Officer, emphasized that the Board's primary responsibility was to ensure pensions could be paid when due and the Fund remained appropriately funded.
findings.matters: Improving pension fund funding reduces future pressure on Windsor and Maidenhead's budget for employer contributions, directly benefiting the council's finances.
findings.figures: Not quantified in the paper; qualitative improvement noted.

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 Pension Schemes Act 2026 compliance update
findings.headline: Two members remain non-compliant with conflicts of interest declarations required under the March 2026 policy.
findings.detail: Following adoption of the Conflicts of Interest Policy in March 2026, members of the Committee, Advisory Panel and Local Pension Board were asked to declare interests. By the report date, two declarations remain outstanding—one from a Committee Member and one from an Advisory Panel Member—despite four reminders (June through August 2026) and individual follow-up from senior officers.
findings.matters: Conflicts of interest declarations are a foundational governance control. Incomplete compliance with a recently adopted policy indicates a gap in implementation of required controls.
findings.figures: 2 declarations outstanding

findings.paper_title: ITEM 6 Pension Schemes Act 2026 compliance update
findings.headline: The council has proposed deletion from its risk register of the risk of being unprepared for Pension Schemes Act 2026 compliance.
findings.detail: The paper reports that work on pooling, investments and governance is now substantially complete, and a risk that was recorded in the June 2026 risk register is proposed to be removed. This indicates the council considers itself prepared for the new regulatory regime and has managed to implement required changes in time.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders want to see that councils implement new regulatory requirements promptly and effectively. Removing a tracked preparedness risk demonstrates the council has managed a significant regulatory change successfully.
findings.figures: Risk was on June 2026 risk register; now proposed for deletion
findings.quote: Based on work carried out to date, detailed in previous committee reports, other items on the agenda for this meeting and information above, it is proposed that this risk be deleted from the risk register.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs are forecasted to overspend by £0.302m with household numbers rising above budget assumptions by year-end
findings.detail: At Month 2 there are 260 households in temporary accommodation against a budgeted assumption of 282. However, the forecast assumes growth to 275 households by year end, compared to a budget assumption of 250, resulting in an unfavourable variance of £0.302m.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a demand-led budget that signals housing stress and rising homelessness. Growth above plan indicates demographic or economic pressures that could continue into future years. It is also volatile and difficult to control.
findings.figures: Current households: 260; budgeted: 282; forecast year-end: 275; budgeted year-end: 250; overspend: £0.302m
findings.quote: At month 2 there are 260 households in temporary accommodation, compared to a budgeted assumption of 282 households. However, the forecast assumes growth to 275 households by year end, compared to a budget assumption of 250 households resulting in an unfavourable variance.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Overdue corporate debt stands at £11.432m (£5.981m over 12 months old) with a significant contractor debt and increasing bad debt provision requirement
findings.detail: Sundry debt arrears have reached £11.432m at 31 May 2026, with £5.981m over 12 months old. The most material issue is £1.197m of unpaid invoices from a significant Place directorate contractor; the council notes discussions are ongoing but payment is not yet confirmed. Additionally, £0.658m is owed by NHS for contributions to care. Bad debt provision is forecast to increase from £5.753m to £6.471m, requiring a £0.692m contribution from revenue budgets.
findings.matters: Large aged arrears (over 12 months) indicate collection difficulty and credit risk. The single large contractor debt is a specific vulnerability; if that payment does not materialise, it will crystallise as a loss. Bad debt provisions consume resources and forecast provisioning suggests confidence in collection is declining.
findings.figures: Total overdue debt: £11.432m; debt over 1 year: £5.981m; contractor debt Place directorate: £1.197m; NHS contributions debt: £0.658m; bad debt provision increase: £0.692m; provision as % of debt: 56.6% (was 58.3% at March)
findings.quote: Overdue debt on the corporate ledger, including deferred payments, at 31 May was £11.432m, with debt over 12 months being £5.981m... The most notable reason for the recent increase in arrears is related to significant contractor in the Place directorate, which has £1.197m of unpaid invoices. Discussions have been ongoing and we anticipate a large amount of this debt being settled imminently.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: Capital programme has identified £12.378m of slippage with execution risk increasing
findings.detail: The 2026/27 capital programme has £12.378m of identified slippage (of which £3.001m is from RBWM-controlled projects). The largest element is £9.377m from the ICB Health Hub due to planned multiyear phasing. Actual expenditure at Month 2 is only 2.6% of forecast. The previous year saw 37% of the budgeted capital programme delay into 2026/27, and the report notes 'there is also an expected risk that the amount of slippage from 2026/27 to 2027/28 (currently 10% of the RBWM controlled projects) will increase.'
findings.matters: Repeated capital slippage (37% last year, further delays expected this year) indicates delivery and project management challenges. Large slippage affects planned savings, service delivery, and funding alignment. It also affects the council's interest and MRP forecasts (lower borrowing due to lower spend means lower financing costs).
findings.figures: Total slippage: £12.378m; ICB Health Hub slippage: £9.377m; actual expenditure Month 2: 1.126m of 43.438m forecast (2.6%); prior year slippage into 2026/27: 37% of budget
findings.quote: Likely slippage of £12.378m has been identified of which £3.001m is presented through RBWM controlled projects. The slippage is principally because of two factors. The most substantial is the planned multiyear phasing of the ICB Health Hub... there is also an expected risk that the amount of slippage from 2026/27 to 2027/28 (currently 10% of the RBWM controlled projects) will increase as the previous year saw approximately 37% of the budgeted capital programme delay into 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant High Needs Block faces a £9.150m overspend with a cumulative deficit projected to reach £17.774m, contingent on government grant write-off
findings.detail: Expenditure on the High Needs education block is forecast at £204.156m against a grant allocation of £195.006m. The cumulative DSG deficit will grow from £8.624m at 31 March 2026 to £17.774m by 31 March 2027. A new High Needs Stability Grant will write off 90% of the deficit (reducing it to £10.012m), but the DfE has confirmed only that it 'will take an appropriate and proportionate approach' to future deficits in 2027/28 and 2028/29 — providing no certainty beyond this year.
findings.matters: This is a structural funding failure: the DSG is frozen in cash terms while SEND demand and costs both rise. The council cannot bridge this gap without government grant. The contingency on the Stability Grant being renewed creates medium-term balance sheet risk.
findings.figures: High Needs Block: £9.150m overspend; cumulative DSG deficit: £8.624m rising to £17.774m; after grant write-off: £10.012m; number of young people with EHCPs: 1,403 (up 86 from 1,317 one year prior)
findings.quote: The 2026/27 pressure on the high needs block is being driven by a mismatch between the grant funding being provided to support services for children with special educational needs and/or disabilities and the cost of support. The grant funding was frozen on a cash basis between 2025/26 and 2026/27 despite increasing numbers of young people becoming eligible for support and inflationary pressures.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Month 2 Budget Management Report Cabinet Briefing
findings.headline: The council remains dependent on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget, and this is described as unsustainable
findings.detail: The report states explicitly that the council 'remains reliant on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget' and that 'Exceptional financial support is not a sustainable solution to the council's financial challenges.' This indicates ongoing structural budget problems that cannot be resolved within normal spending limits.
findings.matters: A council dependent on government bailout funding faces structural credit risk. The reliance suggests either that underlying demand exceeds resources or that service transformation is not progressing. This will need to resolve for the council to be self-sustaining.
findings.figures: EFS forms a significant but unquantified portion of the budget; the report notes the council 'continues to operate within a challenging financial environment'
findings.quote: The Council continues to operate within a challenging financial environment and remains reliant on Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to fund a significant proportion of its budget. Exceptional financial support is not a sustainable solution to the council's financial challenges.

findings.headline: Youth Offending Team relocation tender costs exceed estimate by £0.174m.
findings.detail: The Cranstoun Relocation project, which involves remodelling the Desborough Suite to relocate the Youth Offending Team from Reform Road to Maidenhead Town Hall, is forecasting an overspend of £0.174m because tender evaluation returned bids significantly higher than initially predicted.
findings.matters: Signals weaknesses in project cost estimation during the planning phase. Lenders assess whether the council has reliable project costing and scoping processes, particularly for capital delivery.
findings.figures: £0.174m overspend forecast on relocation remodelling works.
findings.quote: The overspend is projected because the tender evaluation returned bids which were higher than initially predicted.

findings.headline: Stafferton Way Car Park budget increased by £0.200m after survey reveals higher vandalism and additional health & safety works.
findings.detail: Post-budget surveys of Stafferton Way Car Park identified higher levels of vandalism damage than initially assessed and uncovered additional health and safety requirements including replacement of the fire alarm and CCTV systems. This triggered a £0.200m uplift to the project budget.
findings.matters: Illustrates how cost estimating can fall short of actual conditions, requiring significant mid-project increases. The pattern of post-budget cost discovery is relevant to assessing the council's capital project management and delivery capability.
findings.figures: £0.200m uplift required.
findings.quote: A £0.200m uplift to the Stafferton Way Car Park budget has been requested because surveys have determined the level of vandalism to be higher than initially assessed and to encompass an increased scope of works including other health and safety requirements such as a replacement fire alarm and CCTV systems.

findings.headline: School capital allocation cannot be finalized until DfE grant confirmation; £0.363m remains unallocated in April.
findings.detail: The council could not finalize its School Condition Programme budget for 2026/27 until the Department for Education confirmed the grant allocation in April 2026. This left £0.363m of the received grant unallocated four months into the financial year while detailed spending proposals are still being developed.
findings.matters: Demonstrates significant dependency on central government funding timing and creates mid-year budget uncertainty. Cash flow and capital deployment planning cannot be finalized until external grant decisions are made.
findings.figures: £0.363m unallocated; grant confirmation received April 2026.
findings.quote: Budgets were not able to be finalised for 2026/27 until the DfE confirmed the 2026/27 School Condition Allocation which was received April 2026, proposals for the appropriate use of the unallocated sum are being developed.

findings.headline: SEND reform policy pause has deferred £2.338m of High Needs Provision capital investment.
findings.detail: The council was unable to develop capital investment proposals for high needs education provision until the Department for Education released its SEND reforms. Now that these reforms are published, the council plans to bring proposals to Cabinet and public consultation, but this has delayed spending of the full grant allocation to later in 2026.
findings.matters: Shows how external policy decisions create significant delays in council capital planning, affecting when grant funding is actually deployed and impacting cash flow and loan drawdown timing.
findings.figures: £2.338m unallocated from received grant; public consultation planned for later in 2026.
findings.quote: There is £2.338m of the received High Needs Provision Grant currently unallocated because the development of projects was paused as the LA waited for the DfE's SEND reforms. Now that these have been released, the LA will develop proposals for capital investment, to bring to Cabinet and then public consultation, later in 2026.

findings.headline: Housing Service Temporary Accommodation action delayed; progress contingent on recruiting additional staff
findings.detail: The Temporary Accommodation Strategy implementation deadline has slipped from 31 December 2026 to March 2027. The progress update explicitly states that advancement is dependent on recruiting and integrating extra resources into the Housing Service, suggesting current capacity constraints in a potentially high-cost area.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is typically a cost-significant and growing budget pressure for councils. Resource constraints in delivering the strategy suggest the council may struggle to control TA costs and homelessness demand within current staffing levels.
findings.figures: Deadline revised from 31/12/2026 to 31/03/2027
findings.quote: Work on the strategies in officers work programmes but due to capacity issues, progress is dependent on recruiting and integrating extra resources into the Housing Service. This is underway.

findings.headline: Business Continuity Plans only 52% complete; multiple critical service areas still lack current plans
findings.detail: A Priority 1 audit action originally due September 2023 has been extended to July 2026 and remains incomplete. Children services, Communications, Neighbourhood services, and Property have no current plans, and a third of completed plans are out of date. This represents a significant governance gap in operational resilience.
findings.matters: Incomplete business continuity planning exposes the council to operational and service delivery risk. Lenders assessing financial resilience and continuity need confidence in the council's ability to maintain critical functions during disruption.
findings.figures: 52% completion rate; four service areas without current plans
findings.quote: Overall, the percentage of completed Business continuity (BC) plans has slipped slightly from previous reports to 52%. Work continues to be done with various Assistant directors to have their BC plans ready for the start of July. The current areas without a plan that can be shared are Children services, Communications, Neighbourhood services, Property.

findings.headline: Highways inspection and maintenance are under-resourced; we do not have a full complement of staff.
findings.detail: Highways risk rose from 6 to 9 in Q4 and remains at 9 in Q1, above target of 4. The register explicitly states 'We do not have a full complement of staff which is causing issues with the inspection, maintenance and repair of the highway.' An agency inspector commenced mid-June to support, and recruitment for an inspections administrator is progressing, but the gap remains.
findings.matters: Under-resourced highways inspection defers maintenance, increases costs of emergency repairs, and creates liability risk. A staffing gap that requires agency cover is expensive and unstable.
findings.figures: Risk rating Q3 6→Q4 9→Q1 9, target 4; agency inspector commencing mid-June
findings.quote: We do not have a full complement of staff which is causing issues with the inspection, maintenance and repair of the highway.

findings.headline: School building safety risk rating unexpectedly worsened from 4 to 8 in Q1 2026/27.
findings.detail: School building hazards risk rose sharply from 4 to 8 in the latest quarter, a significant deterioration. The risk covers compliance with fire, legionella and asbestos obligations. While the register states ongoing fire surveys, asbestos management and legionella testing are in place, the rating change suggests either new issues have emerged or existing mitigations are not keeping pace with requirements.
findings.matters: A sudden rating rise in school building safety is unusual and suggests a material compliance or resourcing issue has emerged that warrants investigation.
findings.figures: Q3 rating 4, Q4 rating 4, Q1 rating 8
findings.quote: Failure to comply with legislation around and provide a service for monitoring and managing school building related risks such as fire, legionella and asbestos.

findings.headline: Adult safeguarding demand has increased significantly and partnerships are struggling to meet statutory timescales.
findings.detail: Adult safeguarding risk rose from 6 to 9 in Q1 2026/27, moving away from the target of 6. The register notes the council has seen an increase in the number of requests for safeguarding adults reviews and partnerships are under increased pressure to deliver these on time to meet statutory requirements. Work is ongoing to review processes and ensure consistency.
findings.matters: Safeguarding pressure indicates either rising vulnerability in the population or inadequate capacity. Either way, it signals potential service delivery and compliance risk.
findings.figures: Risk rating increased Q3 6→Q4 6→Q1 9, above target of 6
findings.quote: We have seen an increase in the number of requests for safeguarding adults reviews. As a result of these resource demands, partnerships are under increased pressure to get these delivered on time.

findings.headline: Social work and care workforce has 11 vacant posts and recruitment is difficult due to pay scales being uncompetitive.
findings.detail: Workforce stability risk is rated 12/12, well above target of 3. The council faces difficulty recruiting and retaining staff because pay scales are comparatively lower than other local authorities. Adult social care has 11 vacant posts remaining despite salary reviews and retention payments. The council has substantially reduced agency staff but the structural pay competitiveness issue remains. A new workforce plan is in development.
findings.matters: Unfilled social care posts lead to either continued agency spend (which is expensive) or reduced service capacity in a high-risk service. Inability to compete on pay suggests this will persist.
findings.figures: 11 social work posts vacant or covered by locums; 11 vacancies remain in ASCH
findings.quote: Recruitment and stability suffers from comparatively lower pay scales than other local authorities both locally and nationally.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs have been under pressure since 2020/21 and remain at highest risk rating.
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation is rated 12/12, the highest possible risk, with target of 6. Costs have been under pressure for over five years. The council approved a major transformation of housing services in November 2025 to tackle homelessness and reduce reliance on costly temporary accommodation. John West House is complete with services starting early June. Partnership with Registered Housing Providers is in progress and the council is exploring use of its property company, but the risk remains at maximum rating.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is one of the fastest-growing council costs nationally. A five-year trend of pressure and a maximum risk rating indicates the transformation may not be delivering fast enough.
findings.figures: Costs under pressure since 2020/21; John West House services commencing early June 2026
findings.quote: The costs of temporary accommodation could increase beyond the council's capacity to fund. Costs have been under pressure since 2020/21.

findings.headline: Social care market costs are high-risk and ICB is making 50% cuts, threatening jointly funded services.
findings.detail: The social care market risk is rated 12/12 (Q1), above target of 6. The council faces demand pressures for placements in both children's and adults services. The Integrated Care Board is having to make 50% cuts, creating risk that currently funded services may stop or be reduced. The council opened Oak House in-house children's home and has a business case for 22 units of supported accommodation at Imperial Road projected to deliver £216k annual savings.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled placement costs and reductions in joint ICB funding are two of the largest financial exposures facing councils. The council's ability to absorb ICB cuts directly affects social care budget stability.
findings.figures: Projected annual savings approx £216k from Imperial Road accommodation (based on 2025 care prices); ICB 50% cuts
findings.quote: With the ICB having to make 50% cuts there is a risk that currently funded things, even wider than the BCF, may be stopped or reduced.

findings.headline: Pension fund valuation has not improved and remains on track for 2040 full funding only.
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial valuation showed no improvement in the funding level, with the final deficit recovery date remaining static at 2040. The risk is rated 12/12, well above the target of 8. The council is working through options for amending strategic asset allocation, but significant uncertainties remain until the agreed date is reached.
findings.matters: Pension deficits represent long-term obligations that reduce the council's financial flexibility. A static position with no improvement trajectory is concerning.
findings.figures: Deficit recovery date remains 2040; triennial valuation 2025 shows no improvement
findings.quote: The triennial valuation for 2025 has not shown an improvement in the Funding level, but that the final deficit recovery date has remained static at 2040. Significant uncertainties will exist until the agreed date is reached.

findings.headline: In 2028 the DSG statutory override ends, creating an unfunded liability for SEND support.
findings.detail: The DSG (Dedicated Schools Grant) override has masked a deficit in special educational needs funding. It expires in 2028, at which point, if the government takes no action, the council will face severe financial pressures. The risk is rated 12/12, above target of 8, and the council has submitted a Local SEND Reform Plan to access a High Needs Stability Grant to write off 90% of historic deficits accrued by end of 2025/26, but future funding remains uncertain.
findings.matters: This is a known cliff-edge liability in two years' time. If government funding does not materialise, the council faces a structural deficit it cannot absorb.
findings.figures: DSG override due to end 2028
findings.quote: In 2028 the DSG statutory override is due to end. If no further action is taken by govt regarding the funding of support for children and young people with special educational needs or disabilities, this will lead to severe financial pressures.

findings.headline: Council is dependent on exceptional MHCLG financial support with no permanent solution visible.
findings.detail: The council agreed an exceptional financial support package for 2026/27 and is in ongoing dialogue with MHCLG about further exceptional support. The Financial Sustainability risk remains at 16/16, well above the target of 8, with general fund reserves only recently strengthened to circa £16m. Budget dependency on transformation programme delivery creates double risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council's structural budget position has stabilised or is still materially dependent on one-off government grants that may not continue.
findings.figures: General Fund reserves circa £16m
findings.quote: An exceptional financial support package was agreed with MHCLG for 2026/27. Ongoing dialogue with MHCLG covering future exceptional support requirements following authorisation of support for 26/27.

findings.headline: Council implementing 10.6% council tax increase, relying on government removal of referendum principles to enable rise substantially above normal thresholds
findings.detail: The MTFP requires council tax to grow from £110.251m to £121.992m (an increase of £11.741m or 10.6%). This far exceeds the standard 4.99% maximum that would trigger a local referendum. The council can only implement this increase because government has granted it specific exemption from referendum rules for 2027/28 and 2028/29. The paper states the Section 151 Officer and CEO are clear the council must use the full flexibility available to materially improve its position.
findings.matters: The council has exhausted other revenue options; large council tax increases create political and social risk and demonstrate dependency on government goodwill for exceptional flexibility.
findings.figures: Council tax revenue 2026/27 £110.251m; 2027/28 £121.992m; increase £11.741m (10.6%). Standard referendum threshold 4.99%.
findings.quote: Councils are currently only able to increase council tax by a maximum of 4.99% a year without having to hold a local referendum on the proposed increase. The flexibility given to RBWM from government for 2027/28 and 2028/29 means that the council will be able to decide how to set council tax without the need to hold a referendum in either of these years.

findings.headline: Government may require external CIPFA budget reviews and demonstration of all savings avenues explored as conditions for continued Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Access to EFS is conditional on the council proving to government that it has explored every avenue for savings. Beyond this, government reserves the right to impose external CIPFA budget reviews on the council. This creates new governance oversight and potential constraints on council autonomy in financial decision-making.
findings.matters: Government-imposed conditions and external reviews represent new governance risks and may constrain the council's operational flexibility in responding to business changes.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The government may also require that RBWM and any other council needing support to set budgets to be subject to further external budget reviews by CIPFA.

findings.headline: Medium-term funding gap deteriorates from £70.760m to £111.911m by 2030/31; EFS costs rise from 6% to 14% of budget
findings.detail: The MTFP shows the structural problem is not temporary but worsening. The funding gap grows by £41.151m over four years. The cost of government support escalates from £11.895m to £33.481m annually, consuming an increasing share of the budget that could otherwise fund services. By 2030/31, fourteen cents of every pound of council spending will service the cost of previous EFS.
findings.matters: A worsening trajectory indicates the council's structural problems are deepening, not stabilizing, creating long-term financial sustainability risk.
findings.quote: the overall message of a significant structural funding gap remains.

findings.headline: Structural deficit of £70.760m in 2027/28 cannot be closed through transformation, savings and income increases; Exceptional Financial Support from government is essential
findings.detail: The council faces a funding gap of £70.760m in 2027/28 between expenditure of £209.802m and available funding of £139.042m. The paper explicitly states the scale of this deficit cannot be closed through the council's own efforts. Government Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) is not optional but mandatory to balance the budget.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand that the council cannot achieve financial sustainability through operational improvements or savings; viability depends entirely on continued government support.
findings.figures: Opening budget 2027/28 £209.802m; government grants £16.243m; council tax £121.992m; business rates £0.807m; total funding £139.042m; funding gap £70.760m
findings.quote: the scale of the structural budget deficit cannot be closed entirely through transformation, savings and increased income, which means the council – as part of the budget process – will again need to engage with government to agree further EFS.

findings.headline: Medium-term financial forecast is 'extremely difficult' with 'significant funding challenges remaining'
findings.detail: Despite a positive 2025-26 outturn with savings over-delivery of £0.382m, the report explicitly states: 'Over the medium-term, the financial forecast for the council remains extremely difficult, with significant funding challenges remaining'. This is stated as the bottom line position after acknowledging the year's improvements.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's view of its own medium-term trajectory. The council is signalling that one year of improved management does not resolve fundamental structural issues.
findings.figures: Medium-term outlook characterised as 'extremely difficult'
findings.quote: However, this year's outturn has demonstrated a greater level of grip on the financial position, with an overall position of a slight underspend on both service and non-service budgets and an over-delivery of savings. This improved position has allowed some additional financial headroom to be built against future financial shocks. This demonstrates really good progress against annual, in-year budget management. Over the medium-term, the financial forecast for the council remains extremely difficult, with significant funding challenges remaining.

findings.headline: Housing temporary accommodation remains structurally overspent at £1.005m due to 'sustained high presentation of homelessness cases'
findings.detail: Despite reducing actual numbers from 304 forecast to 263 actual households, the service overspent by £1.005m on temporary accommodation due to 'sustained high presentation of homelessness cases and the resulting numbers of households placed in temporary accommodation throughout the year, but particularly in the first six months of the year'. The report notes 'the national trend for the number of households in temporary accommodation is increasing each month'.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost pressure driven by national demand increases. It indicates an area where the council's costs are being pushed by external factors (national homelessness crisis) that cannot be controlled locally.
findings.figures: £1.005m overspend on temporary accommodation
findings.quote: The principal driver of the variance against budget was an overspend on temporary accommodation which was £1.005m over budget due to sustained high presentation of homelessness cases and the resulting numbers of households placed in temporary accommodation throughout the year, but particularly in the first six months of the year. This was partly offset by other items, the most significant being a reduction on the Bad Debt Provision of £0.343m.

findings.headline: Eleven of 34 maintained schools are in deficit (£2.670m negative) while system-wide schools funding pressures mount
findings.detail: Of 34 schools, 11 are in deficit (£2.670m total) while only 23 are in surplus (£2.755m total). The council requires schools in deficit to submit recovery plans and implements 'spending control panel' restrictions on essential items only for severe cases.
findings.matters: Schools in deficit represent both a management and cash flow issue for the council. Systemic school deficits can force council bailouts and squeeze other services.
findings.figures: 11 schools in deficit (£2.670m); 23 schools in surplus (£2.755m)
findings.quote: Of the 34 schools, 11 ended the financial year in a deficit position, totalling a negative balance of £2.670m, while 23 ended the financial year with a positive balance, totalling £2.755m.

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £39.076m (61% of budget) with no delivery on ICB Health Hub (£24.355m) and only 37% overall delivery
findings.detail: The council's capital programme of £64.147m delivered only £23.670m (37%), with £39.076m slippage requested. The ICB Health Hub alone accounts for £24.355m (37% of total slippage) with 0% delivery. Remaining slippage includes schools capital (£5.053m), highways (£4.291m) and Temporary Accommodation (£1.445m). The report notes 'a focus of budget monitoring in 2026/27 will be to provide more challenge on slippage as it is an area of the forecast that clearly needs strengthening'.
findings.matters: Significant capital slippage suggests project delivery or project management issues. For a council under financial stress, inability to spend approved capital (which often comes from grants or borrowing) is a concern - it may indicate planning failures, execution failures, or inability to match project schedules.
findings.figures: £39.076m slippage; £24.355m ICB Health Hub (0% delivery); 37% overall delivery rate
findings.quote: The capital programme shows total slippage requested of £39.076m, predominantly due to the ICB Health Hub (£24.355m). Excluding this project, the remaining £14.721m mainly relates to schools' capital (£5.053m), highways and footway construction (£4.291m), and the Temporary Accommodation Local Authority Housing Fund (£1.445m).

findings.headline: A homecare provider failure is now 'highly likely', with anticipated cost increases in 2026-27
findings.detail: The report notes: 'The risk of failure of a Homecare provider due to difficulties obtaining visas for overseas staff that was highlighted in the Month 10 forecast did not materialise during the year; however, the provider's position has further deteriorated, and the risk of failure is now highly likely. The Commissioning Team have been taking proactive steps to prepare for this, with a change of providers anticipated to increase costs in 2026/27.'
findings.matters: This is an identified cost pressure for 2026-27 in a service (Adult Social Care) that is already overspending. A lender needs visibility of identified future cost pressures.
findings.figures: Anticipated cost increase in 2026-27 (amount not specified)
findings.quote: The risk of failure of a Homecare provider due to difficulties obtaining visas for overseas staff that was highlighted in the Month 10 forecast did not materialise during the year; however, the provider's position has further deteriorated, and the risk of failure is now highly likely. The Commissioning Team have been taking proactive steps to prepare for this, with a change of providers anticipated to increase costs in 2026/27.

findings.headline: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit has worsened from £4.514m to £8.624m, a £4.110m deterioration in one year
findings.detail: The High Needs Block alone overspent by £4.671m (on a budget of £26.587m), driven by 'significant increases in complex children whose education was outside a schools setting (£0.898m), Top-up funding for special schools (£1.108m), Mainstream settings (£0.899m) and placements costs for non-maintained and independent special schools (£1.851m)'. The council notes 'it is recognised nationally that the High Needs system within the Dedicated Schools Grant is failing to fund demand'.
findings.matters: Although the Government has pledged to fund 90% of accumulated deficits through SEND Reforms, the council is currently carrying the full burden of an overspend that is growing year-on-year and is acknowledged to be a national policy failure, not a local management issue.
findings.figures: Opening DSG deficit £4.514m; Closing DSG deficit £8.624m; High Needs Block overspend £4.671m
findings.quote: It is recognised nationally that the High Needs system within the Dedicated Schools Grant is failing to fund demand. There has been a Statutory Override in place for a number of years, which has allowed Councils to hold a 'negative reserve' to fund overspends within the High Needs block.

findings.headline: Children's Services placement costs are rising uncontrollably: £2.275m overspend driven by 'increasing volumes and costs'
findings.detail: Social Care Placements alone overspent by £1.376m and are described as driven by 'increasing volumes and costs'. An additional £0.316m overspend on staffing was needed 'to maintain caseloads'. These are not one-off costs but reflect growing demand. A further £0.305m shortfall exists on Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children grant.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether children's services placement costs are spiralling out of control, and whether savings targets can be met if this directorate is uncontrolled.
findings.figures: £2.275m total Children's Services overspend; £1.376m Social Care Placements overspend; £0.316m staffing pressure; £0.305m UASC shortfall
findings.quote: The primary causes of the overspend are increasing volumes and costs within the Social Care Placements budget, leading to an overspend of £1.376m, and an associated staffing pressure of £0.316m to maintain caseloads.

findings.headline: The council is dependent on Exceptional Financial Support of £39.162m to fund a material portion of its budget
findings.detail: The council received £39.162m in government Exceptional Financial Support in 2025-26, used to offset budget shortfalls. Despite an in-year underspend, the council remains 'in a difficult financial situation and dependent on Exceptional Financial Support to fund a considerable proportion of its budget'. This support reduces by only £1.251m from the £39.162m total even after this year's surplus.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether the council can operate without ongoing government bailout, or whether EFS is structural and indefinite.
findings.figures: £39.162m EFS; only £1.251m reduction in EFS requirement despite £3.079m underspend
findings.quote: notes that in the light of the underspend position, unallocated funds received in year of £1.251m will be used to reduce the level of exceptional financial support applied, which is £39.162m in total

findings.paper_title: 2.a Standard Report Template - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion Report June 2026
findings.headline: Premises Health and Safety compliance remains incomplete with one Priority 1 action outstanding
findings.detail: Identified in 2023/24 as a high-risk area, the council lacks formal agreements defining health and safety expectations for shared premises. Data on statutory compliance is incomplete and out of date, preventing central monitoring. One Priority 1 action remains outstanding as of the 31/07/26 deadline.
findings.matters: Uncontrolled health and safety compliance across council premises creates statutory liability and operational risk. Combined with the pattern of multi-year unresolved audit actions, it signals deeper issues with compliance management.
findings.figures: High risk area; 1 Priority 1, 5 Priority 2 actions outstanding; revised deadline 31/07/26
findings.quote: A key finding was the lack of any agreement in place for premises that are not solely occupied by RBWM staff to define expectations and responsibilities and confirm the Health and Safety Policies that should be followed.

findings.paper_title: 2.a Standard Report Template - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion Report June 2026
findings.headline: Capital Programme Management is receiving Limited Assurance with two Priority 1 (major) audit findings still unresolved
findings.detail: The audit of capital programme management returned a Limited Assurance opinion, indicating improvement is required to effectively manage capital risks. Two Priority 1 recommendations remain outstanding, along with four Priority 2 issues. These were due for completion by 30/11/26 but remain incomplete.
findings.matters: Capital delivery failures directly threaten the council's ability to fund critical infrastructure and regeneration. Priority 1 issues in capital management suggest the council cannot reliably execute major spending commitments.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 1, 4 Priority 2 recommendations; original deadline 30/11/26
findings.quote: Capital Programme Management Final Limited

findings.paper_title: 2.a Standard Report Template - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion Report June 2026
findings.headline: Significant number of audit-recommended actions remain unimplemented beyond their original deadlines, including those tied to high-risk areas
findings.detail: Internal Audit reports that management has struggled to implement agreed actions on time. A significant volume remain outstanding beyond their original implementation dates, specifically including actions relating to areas of high corporate impact risk. This pattern suggests systemic issues with management's capacity or commitment to remediation.
findings.matters: Lenders assess implementation risk heavily—a council unable to execute on its own audit remediation plans is a red flag for financial management capability and follow-through on corrective actions.
findings.figures: 80 total Internal Audit actions outstanding at year-end: 4 Priority 1, 43 Priority 2, 33 Priority 3
findings.quote: a significant number of agreed audit actions remain outstanding beyond their original implementation dates, including some relating to areas of high corporate impact risk

findings.paper_title: 2.a Standard Report Template - Internal Audit Annual Conclusion Report June 2026
findings.headline: Council faces significant underlying financial pressures with historic weaknesses and low financial resilience
